## Artificial neural networks

:::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width=60%}

- A *neural network* is a group of neurons working together in such a persistent state.

::: {.fragment}
- It's really just a big, complicated function, $\mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{in}}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{out}}}$, with lots of parameters ($\theta$). 
  - Built from many smaller units (neurons)
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Input data: some vector of numbers, $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{in}}}$
  - Images (matrix of pixels)
  - Text (strings)
  - Audio signals (time series)...
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Outputs:
  - Boolean, aka classification (cat vs. dog)
  - Number, aka regression
:::

::::

:::: {.column width=40%}
![Diagram of a simple neural network](/assets/07_ml/nn.svg){width=100% fig-alt="Diagram of a simple neural network"}

## MNIST handwriting recognition

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
- Famous example: *USPS handwriting recognition system*
  - Work of UB's Prof. Venu Govindaraju! [Commercializing AI Tech | United States Postal Service](https://www.buffalo.edu/research/research-expertise/case-study-ai-at-usps.html)
- The *MNIST database* is a large, labeled collection of handwritten digits (available from [kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/hojjatk/mnist-dataset))
  - MNIST = Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology
- Good lesson in data cleaning:
  - Starting point: 9,298 digits manually extracted from mail passing through Buffalo USPS in 1989. 
  - Human error rate: 2.5%! Messy data!
  - Original NIST dataset: separate train/test datasets from different populations; 16x16 images; black-and-white. 
  - *M*NIST: uniform train/test sampling; 28x28; anti-aliased/greyscale (each pixel is 0-255). 
:::

:::

# Machine learning basics

---

## Basics

- The concepts behind neural networks are not particularly deep! 
  - "Build a function out of many small functions"
- Nor are neural networks even a particularly new idea!
  - Simplest example: least squares regression (Gauss, 1795!)
  - Perceptron ([1958](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0042519)); multilayer perceptron+stochastic gradient descent ([1967](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/amari1967.pdf)); backpropagation (70/80s); recurrent/convolutional NNs (80/90s)
- So: why are we only experiencing this AI revolution now, in 2026? A few factors:
  - Free availability of large, labeled datasets
  - Free availability of open source languages, libraries, and models
  - ~~Free~~ Wide availability of necessary computing power to train models

::: {.fragment .absolute width="50%" top=0 left=25%}
![NVidia stock](/assets/07_ml/nvidia_stock.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Chart of NVidia stock going through the roof"}
:::

---

## The network

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- The neural network is "just" a function, $\text{NN}_{\theta}$. 
  - Maps $\mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{in}}}\equiv \mathbb{R}^{N_0} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N_L} \equiv \mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{out}}}$
  - Depend on a lot of parameters, $\vec{\theta}$. 
- Construct a complicated function by chaining together many simple functions:
  - $\text{NN}_{\theta} = f^{(L)}_{\theta} \circ f^{(L-1)}_{\theta} \circ .... \circ f^{(2)}_{\theta} \circ f^{(1)}_{\theta}$
  - $f^{(1)}_{\theta}:\ \mathbb{R}^{N_{0}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N_1}$ maps the input ($N_0$-dimensional space) to the first **hidden layer** ($N_1$-dimensional space). 
  - Similarly, $f^{(j)}:\ \mathbb{R}^{N_{j-1}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N_j}$ for $j=2,...,L-1$. 
  - ...and finally, $f^{(L)}:\ \mathbb{R}^{N_{L-1}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N_L}$. 
- The dimensions $N_j$ are *hyperparameters* of the model, describing the shape of the network. 
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![Example neural network](/assets/07_ml/nn_simple.webp){width="95%" fig-alt="Example neural network"}
:::
::::

---

## The neurons

- $\text{NN}_{\theta} = f_{\theta}^{(L)} \circ f_{\theta}^{(L-1)} \circ ... \circ f^{(2)}_{\theta} \circ f^{(1)}_{\theta}$
- The $f^{(j)}$ are **neurons**: the basic units of the neural network. 
  - They should be simple, but not too simple.
  - Specifically, they must be *nonlinear*! 
  - Otherwise, the whole network reduces to a matrix multiplication!

## Activation function

- The activation function can be anything you want, so long as it's nonlinear. Some popular choices:

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width=40%}
```{python}
#| echo: true
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)
y = 1. / (1. + np.exp(-x))
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.title("Sigmoid")
```

:::

::: {.column width=40%}
```{python}
#| echo: true
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)
y = np.where(x > 0, x, 0)
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.title("RELU")
```

:::

## Full network

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width=30%}
- Example of a full neural network.
- Each connection has a weight, $w$. 
- Each neuron has a bias (or offset), $b$. 
- Each neuron has a nonlinear activation function, $f$.
- Values are fed into the input layer, $\mathbb{R}^8$, and the neural network returns values in the output layer, $\mathbb{R}^2$. 
:::

## Evaluating the neural network

![Evaluating the neural network, aka **feed forward**](/assets/07_ml/nn_ff_2.svg){width=55%}

- Form $z$: linear combination using connection weights + bias.
- Apply nonlinear activation: $y = f(z)$.

## Evaluating the neural network

![Evaluating the neural network, aka **feed forward**](/assets/07_ml/nn_ff_3.svg){width=55%}

- Repeat for all neurons in the hidden layer.
- Result: 9 values between 0 and 1 (sigmoid activation), aka "not-fired" and "fired".

## Evaluating the neural network

![Evaluating the neural network, aka **feed forward**](/assets/07_ml/nn_ff_4.svg){width=55%}

- Repeat for all layers until output.
- This process is called **feed forward**.

::: {.absolute top=20% left=5% max-width="25%"}

<span style="color: blue;">Blue=positive</span>

<span style="color: orange;">Orange=negative</span>

## Notation

We use the following notation in these slides:

- $l=0,1,...,L$ indexes the layers.
- $y_i^{(l)}$=output value of neuron $i$ in layer $l$, where $i=1,...,N^{(l)}$. 
  - Special cases: $y_i^{(0)}$=input values, $y_i^{(L)}$=output values.
- $w_{ij}^{(l)}$=weights connecting neuron $j$ in layer $l-1$ to neuron $i$ in layer $l$. 
- $b_{i}^{(l)}$=bias of neuron $i$ in layer $l$. 

The feed-forward evaluation computes:

- $z_{i}^{(l)}=\sum_{j=1}^{N^{(l-1)}} w_{ij}^{(l)} y_j^{(l-1)} + b_i^{(l)}$ (the linear combination of weights).
- $y_i^{(l)} = f(z_{i}^{(l)})$.
  - $f(z)$=nonlinear activation function
  - Typical functions for hidden layers: relu, sigmoid, tanh, ... 
  - Final layer might have a different activation function, e.g., softmax to form "probabilities".

:::: {.columns .vcenter}

::: {.column width=50%}

- Next, let's gain some intuition for "what the network is doing." 
- Consider a very small network: two input neurons, one output neuron, and no hidden layers. 

$$
z = w_1 y_1 + w_2 y_2 + b
$$

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

![z value with 2 inputs. This is just a plane.](/assets/07_ml/surface_z.svg){width=95% fig-alt="z value with 2 inputs is just a plane"}

:::

## A very simple network

:::: {.columns .vcenter}

::: {.column width=50%}

- Next, let's gain some intuition for "what the network is doing." 
- Consider a very small network: two input neurons, one output neuron, and no hidden layers. 

$$
\begin{aligned}
z &= w_1 y_1 + w_2 y_2 + b \\
f(z) &= 1 / (1 + e^{-z}) 
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.fragment .callout-note}
- Intuition: neuron acts as a "step function", here in 2D because we have 2 input neurons.
:::

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

![Sigmoid neuron output from 2 inputs](/assets/07_ml/surface_sigmoid.svg){width=95% fig-alt="Sigmoid neuron output from 2 inputs"}

:::

::::

## Function approximation

- So far, it is probably not obvious why NNs are useful.
  - Simple example: (2 inputs, 1 output) = step function in 2D
- An important result: NNs can (in principle) approximate any continuous function! 
  - "Universal approximation theorems"
- Let's examine one formulation in detail: a feedforward NN with a single hidden layer, with *nonlinear* activation functions, can act as a *universal approximator*. 
  - [Cybenko, "Approximation by superpositions of a sigmoidal function", 1989](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02551274)

::: {.callout-warning}
- This is only an existence theorem! Existence does not help you make a good/efficient neural network. 
:::

## Building the approximation

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width=50%}
![First 2 steps](/assets/07_ml/uat_build_2_annotated.svg){width=90% fig-alt="Approximating a function: first two steps"}

$$
y_{\text{out}} = \delta F_0 + \delta F_1 f(w\cdot(y-Y_1)) + \delta F_2 f(w\cdot(y-Y_2))
$$

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

::: {.fragment}
![2-step neural network](/assets/07_ml/uat_build_2_nn.svg){width=50% fig-alt="Neural network approximating 2 step functions with 1 input, 2 hidden neurons, and 1 output"}

- Hidden neurons: 
  - Biases $b_i = -w Y_i$
  - $f$=sigmoid (the larger $w$, the sharper the turn-on)
- Output neuron: no activation, bias=$\delta F_0$
:::
:::
::::

:::

## Approximating a 2D function

- Approximating functions in higher dimensions is a bit trickier, but basically the same concept. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=60%}
- 1D step function: 

$$
f(x; x_0) = \left\{\begin{matrix} a & : & x > x_0 \\ b & : & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix} \right.
$$

- 2D step function:

$$
f(x, y; x_0, y_0) = \left\{\begin{matrix} a & : & (x>x_0) \&\& (y > y_0) \\ b & : & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix} \right.
$$

- In terms of neurons: 
  - Implement 1D step functions for $y_1>Y_1$ and $y_2>Y_2$, both with height 1.
  - Add them up: possible values are 0, 1, or 2.
  - Pass sum through another step function: inactive for 0, 1, and active for 2.
  - Note: this is basically an `AND` gate! 
:::

::: {.column width=40%}
![2D step function](/assets/07_ml/uat_2dstep.svg){width=70% fig-alt="2D step function"}
:::
::::

- Build the 2D function one block at a time, using 2D step functions

## Recap

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=60%}
- Neural networks are arbitrarily large functions built from very simple pieces: **neurons**.
- Each neuron:
  - Calculates a linear combination of inputs from the previous layer: $z_j = \sum_k w_{jk} y_k^{\text{in}} + b_j$
  - Applies a *nonlinear* activation function: $y_j = f(z_j)$. 
- The nonlinearity is essential: otherwise we are just doing linear algebra!
- **Universal approximation theorems**: NNs can approximate arbitrary continuous functions.
  - Conceptually simple proof.
  - Warning: statement of existence, does not tell you how actually to build a NN. 
  - Also, we usually doing much more complicated tasks than just approximating functions. But nonetheless, it demonstrates the power of NNs: they can create arbitrarily complicated functions of the inputs.

:::

::: {.column width=40%}
![One layer of a neural network](/assets/07_ml/nn_2_to_3.svg)
:::
::::
